subcategory: native perennial (longleaf pine savanna Hibiscus selection)

planting.note: Plant divisions or potted stock in spring once soil has warmed, into moist to wet, acidic, sandy soil in full sun; mulch the root crown lightly in zone 7 winters.

directions: 'Brunswick' is a 2006 Plant Delights Nursery introduction propagated from a wild population in Brunswick County, North Carolina, where the species grows in upland bogs, roadside ditches, and wet longleaf pine coastal pinelands. From early summer into fall, leaf axils along the fuzzy, okra-like stems produce 4-5 inch, cone-shaped, light yellow flowers with a dark purple eye. Grow in consistently moist to seasonally wet, acidic, sandy soil in full sun; the deciduous clump dies back in winter and resprouts vigorously in spring. Excellent for rain gardens, cut flowers, and longleaf savanna restoration plantings; attracts hummingbirds and butterflies and tolerates coastal salt spray.

subcategory: native perennial (longleaf pine savanna Marshallia selection)

planting.note: Direct sow in fall into moist to wet, sandy, acidic, nutrient-poor soil; avoid fertile or amended beds, which suppress flowering.

directions: 'Georgetown' is a 2025 Plant Delights/Juniper Level Botanic Garden introduction grown from a Zac Hill/Patrick McMillan seed collection made in Georgetown County, South Carolina, where this coastal-plain-endemic Marshallia grows in full sun on seasonally flooded but always-moist sandy savanna soils. Narrow, grass-like basal foliage sends up 20-inch flower spikes beginning in early-to-mid June, each topped with a frilly, lavender-and-white, powder-puff composite flower head. Keep soil consistently moist and lean; this selection is an excellent, still rarely grown addition to wet garden margins, bog gardens, and longleaf pine savanna restoration plantings, and makes an unusual cut flower.

subcategory: native wildflower (longleaf pine savanna gentian relative)

planting.note: Sow seed on the surface of moist, sandy or peaty soil in spring; seed is tiny and light-dependent for germination, so do not cover, and keep the seedbed consistently damp.

directions: 'Santa Rosa' is a 2023 Plant Delights/Juniper Level Botanic Garden introduction grown from nursery seed sourced by plantsman John Hummer from a population in Santa Rosa County, Florida. This diminutive rosegentian naturally occurs in coastal savannas from South Carolina west to Texas, forming a low basal rosette only a couple of inches tall from which upright, branched flowering stalks rise to about 8 inches, topped from mid-June onward with 2-inch pink, daisy-like flowers with a bright yellow eye. Site it in a seasonally moist bog garden or a consistently damp spot mimicking its wet savanna habitat; it is a strong butterfly and native-bee nectar source and pairs well with pitcher plants and sundews in a constructed bog planting.

subcategory: native perennial (longleaf pine savanna goldenrod selection)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring into full sun, sandy, damp soil; established clumps are surprisingly drought-tolerant despite the species' wet native habitat.

directions: 'Golden Voices' is a 2025 Plant Delights/Juniper Level Botanic Garden introduction selected from a Beaufort County, North Carolina population of this little-grown coastal goldenrod, a species formally distinct from the already-cataloged Solidago stricta despite sharing the 'wand goldenrod' common name in some casual sources. Large basal rosettes send up narrow, rod-like, unbranched flowering spikes that can reach 6 feet, opening into slender wands of small gold flowers from late summer into October. Native to longleaf pine savannas, flatwoods, and damp sandy coastal-plain soils from North Carolina to Louisiana, it tolerates average garden conditions once established and is a strong late-season nectar source for native bees, butterflies, and migrating songbirds; works well toward the back of a bog garden or wet meadow planting alongside pitcher plants.
sources: Flora of the Southeastern United States (FSUS)
